style: prop (Trillium), discretionary intraday, capitulation/reversal and breakout specialist
edge_principles: Broken slot machine: each day only ~5-10 names in the whole market offer real edge; trade those rather than a fixed favourite niche, and pick the most extreme instance of a theme (biggest dislocation vs its driver/the index).
Require alignment across timeframes (intraday and daily both a buy) before taking a trade; skip when the move is already too extended for the with-trend side.
Judge moves by price over time (speed/size of the move) plus volume capitulation, not by price level alone.
Grade setups A/B/C and pre-set risk per grade on a card; stop trading C setups entirely and scale risk exponentially (not linearly) on A/A+ setups.
Default stop is the prior bar low (long) / prior bar high (short) on the short intraday chart.
The same price has different expected value at different moments: a breakout or news reaction bought late after it has come back is a worse trade than the first print.
Do not exit at the first higher-low pullback after a confirmed breakout; give the trade to the real low (channel fundamentals).
Process: one-goal daily report card, detailed write-ups and screen recordings of only the biggest plays, mentor feedback; lockouts after ~3 losing trades to avoid tilt.
notes: Part 3 interview recorded June 2022: broken slot machine stock selection, right side of the V capitulation entries, channel fundamentals and exponential bet sizing. Mentions an index stat: ~30 historical cases of a 10% Nasdaq drop in 3 days showed a positive bounce edge.

style: journalist/author (biography of bond fund manager Bill Gross, PIMCO)
edge_principles: Structural alpha: small, repeatable basis-point edges from contract details (e.g. investing idle cash collateral behind futures in short floating notes) compound over years.
Read new contracts carefully: newly launched products can carry embedded options that nobody has priced for an untested regime.
Risk down early into a perceived bubble and accept underperformance; the payoff is having dry powder to buy forced sellers' assets at a discount.
Size and new-issue allocation can be an edge in bond markets, unlike in nimble equity trading.
notes: Author interview about PIMCO and Bill Gross history (GNMA futures trade, 2008 GSE bet, 2014 departure). No intraday setups.

guest: Public Service Announcement (Aaron Fifield, Tessa Dao)
style: host announcement
edge_principles: New co-host attributes her turnaround to reviewing her own trades, managing risk better, simplifying and trading less, and not relying solely on trading income (reduces pressure).
notes: Host transition announcement; co-host briefly mentions neutral multi-leg options trades around earnings. No concrete setups.

style: retail, discretionary intraday large-cap equities (formerly options scalper)
edge_principles: Keep a position-size table next to the screen: account value x risk% / stop distance gives shares instantly; size grows organically with the account.
Default risk 0.5% per trade, 1% only on the best setups; cutting risk in half from 1% fixed his inability to hold trades.
Top-down prep: indexes (SPX, QQQ, IWM, Dow) then sector ETFs (XLE, XLK) to find who leads/lags, then names with catalysts.
Tighten stops in equities to keep reward:risk >= 3-4:1 on realistic intraday ranges.
In choppy bear tape avoid both chasing breakouts and pressing shorts after big declines; fade strength into levels instead.
Most P&L comes from the first couple of hours after the open.
notes: First-year full-time retail trader; ~50% win rate with ~30% scratches. Mostly round-number and post-run fades in large caps.

style: retail/educator (Simpler Trading), discretionary options swing and day trader
edge_principles: Only trade a stock if it is outperforming the index; otherwise just trade the index. On down days scan for stocks that are up and vice versa.

Know when big 'focus trades' are available (strong index + strong stocks, as in 2020-21) and do not force them in choppy regimes; switch to day trading / small weekly goals when swing trades stop working.
'True/false statement': stay in a losing-but-valid setup as long as the original reasons remain true and risk is within plan; exit when a reason becomes false.
Traders tend to make money in the morning and give it back in the afternoon (impatience, decision fatigue); step away from screens.
Never hold directional trades through earnings; momentum often runs into earnings, not through them.
Scale into high-conviction trades (start ~5%, build toward 25-30% of account) using defined-risk spreads so the position can survive sideways chop.
A paper loss equals a real loss; cut non-working trades rather than waiting to get back to even.
Skim profits into illiquid tangible assets so a drawdown cannot give back everything.
notes: Follow-up interview on his 2020-21 big options trades (Tesla, Google). Core setup: relative strength vs weak index + daily squeeze, target 3 ATR Keltner.

style: former CME eurodollar options / NYMEX nat gas floor trader; now discretionary VIX term-structure vs ES trader
markets: rates options, natural gas, VIX futures, ES futures
edge_principles: Some top floor traders made their money fading large spikes up or down (buying the bottom of a flush when many are trapped), contrary to 'never fade' folklore; rules are flexible by trader.
Do not exit a strong trend trade early just because the P&L looks big ('if the train is going to California don't get off in Chicago').
Avoid carrying large option positions into December/holiday illiquidity; short-premium books can lose years of gains quickly.
Vol products (VIX curve, term structure) tend to react first; watching them helps time ES even if you do not trade them.
Common trait of great traders: unflappable, even-keeled under loss; humour as a stress outlet.
New retail traders should treat trading as a part-time job with other income to remove pressure.
notes: Colourful floor-trading war stories (eurodollar pit, Amaranth blowup). Current approach (VIX term structure spreads vs ES levels, wait for extremes) described only vaguely; no concrete setups.

style: fund (Ambrus Group long-volatility tail-risk fund) with intraday flow-based absolute-return book; ex-prop (Chimera)
markets: SPX/VIX options, variance swaps, US stocks intraday
edge_principles: Fund tail hedges (sub-5-delta 1-3 month options, ~10% of AUM) with uncorrelated intraday flow strategies that are flat by the close, rather than by selling concave short-vol structures.
Execution price matters enormously on cheap tails: filling at 5c instead of 20c turns a 5x into a 20x payoff.
Research hygiene: start from a thesis, use 3-4 features max, keep an untouched out-of-sample set; avoid iterative 'what if I had done X' overfitting.
Technical patterns can be valid as the visual form of underlying flow/statistical effects (e.g. VWAP crossovers after institutional buying ends).
Size with fractional Kelly plus a hard cap; scale up slowly when trading well and down when trading poorly.
Markets are not Gaussian; mean-reversion trades that assume known sigma levels are dangerous.
notes: Long-vol fund manager. One concrete intraday flow pattern: large opening drop on bad news attracts dip-buying via MOO/VWAP orders for ~first hour, then fades all day.

style: systematic trend follower; ran a manual DAX warrant volatility arbitrage 2015-2019
markets: German DAX bank-issued warrants vs Eurex DAX options
edge_principles: Structural edges come from counterparties' operational constraints (stale vol surfaces, too-tight retail spreads), not prediction; they decay once the counterparty notices (spread 1c->2c killed it).
Measure relative cheapness intraday with rolling percentiles of the spread to fair value and only act in the extreme decile plus a catalyst (market move).
Paper-trade ~100-200 instances to rehearse execution before going live on an execution-sensitive edge.
Commission and spread sensitivity is decisive for very short holding periods; shop execution venues.
Hide footprint: split legs across counterparties.
notes: Detailed account of a niche retail-structured-product volatility arbitrage. Not transferable to MCF data, recorded for completeness and as an example of a structural edge and its decay.

style: retail, discretionary sector-relative stock trader since the 1990s; now crypto/DeFi yield
edge_principles: Never meet a margin call; exit instead (a short that tripled on fluff news would have wiped him out even though the stock later went to zero).
Follow the stop side of the trading plan rigidly; allow flexibility only on the profit side.
Time stop: exit if the position has not moved above entry within a set period.
Scale in small (e.g. 10% of intended size) and add only as the position proves itself.
Avoid buying stocks in steady downtrends; wait for a bottom/rebound and a catalyst.
Big early wins breed overconfidence and oversizing; behaviour before blow-ups (revenge trading, bigger size, faster trading) is predictable.
notes: New host introduction interview. One loosely specified idea: sector leader moves first and laggards follow days later.

style: fund/CTA, contrarian positioning trader (COT-based) with discretionary overlay
markets: futures: stock indices, currencies, bonds, commodities
edge_principles: Use participation (money actually committed, e.g. COT speculator positioning indexed to its own history) as the discounting mechanism, not price or surveys.
Never act on the crowding signal alone; wait for market confirmation (a news-failure event).
Win rate ~37% with ~4:1 payoff is enough; accept repeated stop-outs while the crowded condition persists.
Treat highly correlated positions as one trade and cut per-trade risk accordingly.
Exit when the crowd is no longer crowded (positioning mean-reverts to neutral) rather than riding to the opposite extreme; volatility rises faster than return after neutral.
His fully systematic version underperformed his discretionary-overlay version; he skips ~20-25% of system signals in known weak spots.
Patience pays: a month away from the screen with a stop made more than a year of in-and-out trading.
notes: Unknown Market Wizards contrarian. Core idea: fade extreme speculator positioning only after a bearish (bullish) headline fails to move price; holds 2-4 months.

style: crypto infrastructure founder (bloXroute), not a trader
edge_principles: Small accounts that churn in and out of trends lose; larger capital held with patience behaves better (he lost by trading instead of holding).
In DeFi, transaction costs are large relative to small positions, which forces fewer, larger moves.
Concentrated AMM liquidity provision is economically a short option (like selling puts/calls in a range); you end up holding the losing asset when price exits the range.
Speed of information (network latency) is an edge in on-chain trading, as in traditional HFT.
notes: DeFi primer (AMMs, liquidity provision, staking, the Merge). No trading setups.

style: retail/small fund FX trader using proprietary retail-positioning and stop-cluster data ('market causality'); also runs ~8 automated FX bots
edge_principles: Retail ('dumb money') tends to try reversals/mean-reversion and place stops just beyond the obvious recent high/low; those clusters get run before the real move.
Expect several counter-moves (he estimates 8-10) and long sideways time before the main run to a known stop cluster; enter with limit orders on counter-moves rather than chasing.
On news, price often spikes to take a nearby stop cluster then reverses back toward where crowded positions are trapped.
Always use a stop (or hedge) and low leverage; going stopless to avoid hunts leads to blowups.
Automated strategies: aim for net profit 2-4x max drawdown over ~8 years of data including variable spread, slippage and commissions; avoid commercial EAs (often martingale).
Stand aside when it is unclear which way the dominant players will push.
notes: Forex 'stop hunting' / smart-money narrative relying on proprietary retail positioning feeds. One price-only analogue (failed range break after stop run) is testable on stocks/ETFs.

style: fund (two small options hedge funds), systematic option seller
edge_principles: 'Expectancy hacking': fix the win/loss size ratio mechanically (profit target and stop as % of credit), then only the win rate determines expectancy; verify it is above break-even by backtest and live trading.
Bake slippage and gap-through-stop losses into the expected loss size instead of rejecting stops.
Credit targeting: size each entry to a constant premium/risk amount (fewer contracts when IV is high) to remove sequence/path risk from variable trade sizes.
Top-down sizing: annual P&L target / expected capture rate / number of trading days = per-trade risk budget.
A stop is just an exposure adjustment; systematic re-entry each day is equivalent to rolling.
Know total open risk: if every open position hit its stop, what % of the account would be lost.
Volatility drag: large drawdowns destroy compounding regardless of edge, so size for the path not only the destination.
notes: Systematic SPX short-put programme with mechanical profit-take and stop; mostly options-specific risk management lessons.

style: retail day trader (penny stocks/OTC and small caps, momentum and fades)
markets: US small caps, OTC penny stocks, TQQQ/SQQQ
edge_principles: Trade only the most active names by dollar volume; liquidity limits slippage and lets you exit when wrong.
Prefer names whose daily candles have full bodies (open near low, close near high); avoid wicky/choppy histories which caused his biggest losses.
Scale size with recent results and market heat: size up in hot periods, down when losing; one hot month can make the year.
Cap position size relative to liquidity (e.g. <= ~$100-150k in illiquid names); two of his biggest losses came from size too big for the volume and from shorting illiquid parabolic scams.
After a stock proves untradeable (gappy, wide spread), stop trading it.
Expensive borrow makes multi-day penny-stock shorts unattractive; capture the one-day dump instead.
Hot speculative regimes are seasonal (Dec-Feb strongest for OTC); do not force your specialty in dead regimes.
No leverage on day trades.
notes: Turned ~$20-30k into ~$11M profits trading low-priced momentum. Three core patterns: pullback breakout, first-red-day short after multi-day run, panic dip buy.

style: retail/educator, systematic intraday futures day trader (42 years)
edge_principles: Pick robust parameters from the middle of a plateau ('island of safety') of working settings rather than the single best backtest.
Do not trust a pattern from a handful of observations (her first 'Friday down -> Monday up' idea failed immediately).
Only take band-to-band trades when the band width offers enough reward to beat costs; she tracks a 'potential hourly wage' per chart.
Flat at end of day; no overnight futures exposure because of overseas news gaps.
Observation: the US open often moves opposite to the overnight session's direction.
Daily post-session chart review: what did I expect vs what happened.
notes: Trades one proprietary adaptive-MA band system on 1/5-min ES for ~35 years; older ADX+MACD 15-min system also mentioned.

style: crypto quant/arbitrage trader, small fund (Luxembourg)
markets: crypto spot and perpetual futures, DeFi
edge_principles: Latency-sensitive arbitrage (triangular, cross-exchange) decays as professional market makers arrive; shift to non-latency-sensitive edges.
Order-flow edge: look for trapped participants (positions now under water in unfavourable conditions) and trade their forced exits.
When markets are quiet and edges thin, do not force trades; build systems and wait for volatility.
Diversify counterparty risk across venues (exchange failure like FTX); use leverage mainly to limit capital parked on any one venue.
Microservice system design so one failed component does not halt trading.
notes: Crypto quant; main described edge is cross-exchange perpetual funding-rate arbitrage (delta neutral). Not applicable to MCF stock data.

style: trading psychology coach; systematic rule-based trader running a small fund
edge_principles: Most execution errors (moving stops, hesitating, cutting winners early, FOMO entries) stem from intolerance of uncertainty; treat each outcome as quasi-random within a positive-expectancy system.
Prefer rule-based systematic trading to discretion because human biases erode discretionary results.
Judge yourself on behavioural consistency with the rules, not P&L per trade; consistency of behaviour produces consistency of results.
Size so you care but are not destabilised; keep per-trade risk small to survive long enough for the edge to play out.
Build accountability (journal, group, external review) to replace the institutional risk manager retail traders lack.
Daily pre-market meditation (20-30 min) to build equanimity.
Aim for steady 10-30% annual returns rather than boom-bust years.
notes: Psychology-focused episode (uncertainty, mindfulness, accountability). No concrete setups.

style: quant hedge fund manager (Palomar Capital), short-term systematic futures/equity trader, finance professor
edge_principles: Many backtested edges vanish once transaction costs are included; require profits that overcome costs and compensate for risk.
If a result looks too good to be true, check the code for look-ahead bias first.
High win-rate strategies often hide rare large losses; examine the tail.
Edges get crowded and decay (convertible arb, growth/FANG); spend most time (~90%) researching new ideas and keep monitoring retired strategies, which can revive.
Strategy performance depends on emotional/volatility regimes; model which strategies work in which volatility environment.
Shorting is swimming upstream; reduce short exposure in falling-rate cycles, be more willing to short in hiking cycles; profits in down markets often come from buying the bounces.
Systems should stop trading when moves become extreme enough that trades may be busted (flash-crash lesson).
The best trades are often the ones that feel most uncomfortable to place.
notes: Quant fund manager and market historian. Mostly research-process principles; one regime filter idea for short exposure.

style: retail-turned-manager, rules-based trend follower ('trading boxes'); swing stocks, day-trades ES
edge_principles: Treat support/resistance as zones (a band, e.g. +/-1 point around a level), not lines; when a zone breaks, expect travel to the next zone.
Use a key higher-timeframe zone as a risk-on/risk-off filter: above it favour longs, below it favour shorts or cash.
Only take A+ setups that meet every requirement; patience (no trade if no setup) was his turning point.
Study the few recurring post-breakout paths (straight run, choppy grind, retest of the box then continuation) through backtesting so position size and holding are not driven by fear.
Higher risk per trade (he uses ~4% on ES day trades, ~5% on 'all-in' swing trades) multiplies returns and drawdowns (15% drawdown in 2022); only sizes up when all conditions are met.
The same structure-based strategy works on daily and 5-minute charts.
notes: Managed account up ~64% in 2020 and ~200% day-trading ES in 2022 per guest (unverified). Core setup: month-long squeeze box around the 50-day MA, trade the break in the 50-day MA's direction to the next zone.

style: retail full-time day/swing trader (One Option community; r/RealDayTrading founder), ex-statistics professor
edge_principles: Trade stocks with relative strength/weakness versus SPY in the direction of the market: the market is the wind; a stock already strong against a headwind runs with a tailwind.
Follow institutional money: require volume confirmation on breaks of key levels; retail cannot sustainably move stocks.
Not all S/R is equal: 200/100/50-day SMAs and high-volume-anchored trend lines matter more than fast EMAs or Fibonacci.
In macro-driven regimes (Fed, CPI, yields) context matters more than pure chart checklists; know the macro calendar.
Learning path: ~6 months study, then paper trade until 75% win rate and profit factor >= 2 for 3 consecutive months, then trade 1 share and repeat the benchmark (~2 years total).
Exits on chart/thesis invalidation, not on P&L; add to winners rather than taking profits early.
Treat trading as a business with monthly expectancy targets; raise base capital ~15% every six months.
Small accounts: take only the one or two highest-probability trades a day, often as defined-risk spreads.
Backtests are easily overfit; useful mostly for rejecting ideas.
notes: Relative strength vs SPY day/swing trader; describes algo lines (trend lines anchored on high-volume days) and a far-OTM put credit spread below stacked support.

style: neurophysiologist / performance coach (not a trader)
edge_principles: Sleep is the main performance lever for decision quality: consistent ~10pm-6am schedule, dark cool room, no alcohol (suppresses REM, which regulates emotions), no caffeine after ~2-3pm, last meal ~2 hours before bed.
Chronic stress, sleep debt and drinking measurably age the frontal lobe that handles decision making; P&L leaderboards and post-close drinking are a bad combination.
Exercise: ~20 minutes of cardio daily plus ~3 resistance sessions a week (compound lifts ~70% of 1RM); heart rate variability as a recovery gauge.
Morning bright light (or a 10,000 lux lamp) anchors the circadian rhythm.
Build habits by repetition; consistency matters more than intensity.
notes: Brain/health episode; no trading content beyond performance-maintenance advice.

style: retail full-time short seller (small caps, pump-and-dumps, fraud research)
edge_principles: Float filter for shorts: avoid floats < ~3M (squeezable, expensive borrow); 10-20M float is the low-hassle sweet spot.
Borrow-fee filter: skip (or only trade early) when IBKR borrow fee > ~200%; a sudden jump in borrow fee intraday warns of a coming squeeze.
Avoid shorting names with high institutional ownership; VWAP-buying algos stop them breaking down.
No new short entries after ~11:00 ET in hard-to-borrow names; mostly cover intraday, avoid overnight borrow and buy-in risk.
Short the sympathy plays rather than the 'head of the snake'; never fight a crowd-driven mania however absurd.
Forced buy-ins cluster around broker check times (~3pm and after the close); large sudden prints into a spike often mean a short being liquidated - more may follow.
Lifestyle changes (no alcohol, routine around pre-market hours) supported consistency.
notes: Retail short seller who also does on-site fraud investigations (Flora Growth). Setups: post-lockup midday spike short, fluffy-biotech-news spike short, paid-promotion pump short after the crack.

style: retail options/index trader turned risk-management educator (TraderHelp101)
edge_principles: Plan for the speed of losses, not just their size: know what event makes a trade a loser and how fast the planned loss can arrive, so you do not freeze.
'Block trading': evaluate risk over a block of ~15 trades and ask where the account would be if all 15 lost; size so a full losing streak is survivable.
Grade losses: planned, respectable (a small allowance beyond plan), embarrassing, devastating; never let one become the last two.
Split a learning account into several sub-accounts (e.g. $10k into 5 x $2k) so each acts as a hard account-level stop and extends learning time.
Prefer one-to-one risk (capital committed equals max loss) over 'partial risk' that relies on discretionary exits while learning.
Learning in a volatile regime (2008) distorts expectations of normal ranges.
Income pressure (needing trading to pay bills) drives reckless sizing and holding losers; keep other income streams.
Daily stop and emotional-trigger rules; accountability partner.
notes: Story of a full-time trader who went broke in 2008-09 from oversizing and compulsive trading; risk-management and psychology lessons, no concrete setups.

style: retail-turned-professional, data-driven small-cap short seller ('agenda trading') with pyramiding; later mid/large-cap swing longs
markets: US small caps (short), mid/large caps (swing long)
edge_principles: Validate a setup by building a scan/bucket that isolates it; from the bucket compute average open->high-of-day, high->low, open->close moves and trade the 'average chart': enter near the typical HOD, target the typical LOD, stop where price diverges from the average path.
Combine setup-level odds with stock-specific history (same underwriter/operators tend to move a stock the same way each time).
'Agenda': know why a move should happen (company needs cash, has a shelf/ATM, history of raising) to hold through counter-moves with confidence.
Pyramid into winners: small starter, cut quickly if wrong (max ~3 attempts per day then stop trading), add aggressively as the fade confirms, trailing the stop so adds do not reduce the odds.
Most profits come from a few days (~5% of days give ~90% of gains): size by setup grade and press on the rare A+ days rather than trading linearly every day.

Edges come and go with regimes (QE-era small-cap dilution boom); track setup statistics as a rolling series and step back when range/follow-through shrink - drawdowns come from noticing regime change late.
Profit factor (win rate x payoff) is what matters, not either alone.
Avoid fat-tail (black swan) exposure from oversizing illiquid shorts even at the cost of lower returns.
Weekly/monthly/yearly reviews; positive 'punishment' (extra review, exercise) for rule breaks; trusted peer pod for honest feedback.
notes: Audited 2020 performance claimed extraordinary. Core: dilution-driven small-cap gapper shorts using statistical average-path entries/targets and pyramiding; also failed range-breakout shorts and up-to-4-day swing shorts.

style: discretionary intuitive scalper (16+ years), ran a small private fund; trades US stocks/futures from Germany
markets: US stocks, Nasdaq micro futures (MNQ), earnings movers
edge_principles: Have a live audio news squawk running: headline shocks move index futures before most participants react.
Focus on one instrument at a time; average hold ~5 minutes; take the first move and re-enter for the second.
Move stop to break-even quickly once a trade works (he reports 80-90% win rate, many scratches).
Cut losses fast - letting losers run blew up his personal accounts ~50 times.
Investors anchor on recent returns: deliver steady small gains rather than big spikes that raise expectations and push risk-taking.
Daily transparent reporting to investors builds trust.
Caution: his all-in, single-position sizing and frequent strategy switching are high-risk practices.
notes: Highly discretionary, feel-based scalper; describes shorting MNQ on a fake 'Pentagon explosion' headline and trading earnings-release spikes; no rule-based setups beyond news reaction.

style: retail full-time day trader / YouTuber; moved from small caps to large-cap catalyst stocks
markets: US stocks (large caps, formerly small caps)
edge_principles: Journal-derived rule: stop after 3 losing trades on a red day (her red days had 6-7 trades vs ~4 on green days; deleting trades after the 3rd loss shrank red days a lot).
Trade only the first ~2.5-3.5 hours (to ~12:00-13:00 ET); later trading gave back profits.
Fix a constant dollar risk per trade (size = risk / stop distance); daily max loss ~2x the per-trade risk.
Increase size only on the specific setups the journal shows earn 3-4R, and raise size gradually (e.g. +20-50% steps over weeks).
Dropping small caps cut stress and losses with little P&L sacrifice once she reviewed the numbers; avoid overnight holds in headline-driven markets.
Never turn a day trade into a swing / add to a loser (her biggest loss: a short in an uptrending stock held two months).
Have a full year of living expenses saved separately before going full-time.
notes: Retail day trader; bread-and-butter is large-cap earnings gap-up dip buy back to premarket high, plus shorting bounces after broad earnings misses.

style: retail index-futures day traders (prop-firm evaluation journey); community recording
markets: NQ/MNQ, ES, YM, DAX, FTSE futures/CFDs
edge_principles: Read prop-firm fine print (trailing drawdown definition, news bans, consistency/'gambling' rules, payout schedules, activation fees) and pick a firm whose rules fit your style.
Intraday trailing drawdown (measured from peak unrealised equity) punishes giving back open profit: take profits quickly, re-enter on the next break, keep peak-to-current gap small.
Cheap evaluation accounts breed gambling habits; treat them like real capital.
Move stops to break-even as soon as the break shows hesitation; accept several scratches before catching the runner rather than full-size losses.
US session (15:30-22:00 CET) offers far better index-futures opportunity than the European morning.
Level 2, time & sales, options flow and an audio news squawk add context to price-action entries.

Patrick averages into losers with a doubling ladder (1-2-4-8 contracts within a set max, abandoning beyond ~40-50 ticks); he admits this blew up many accounts - a high-ruin practice that MCF should not copy.
Backtests on paper overstated live performance roughly 2x for the newer trader.
notes: Community Zoom discussion about passing a futures prop-firm evaluation. Concrete-ish ideas: index divergence (NQ vs ES) short when the stronger index fails at resistance, and 1-min 20-SMA hold/fail.

style: ex order-flow futures scalper; co-founder of a fully automated crypto fund (market-neutral + long/short momentum)
markets: crypto spot/perps/futures; formerly ES, NQ, YM, DAX, Nikkei, RBOB/heating oil spreads
edge_principles: Psychology issues shrink when the strategy has a verifiable edge; a lot of 'psychology' blame covers strategies with no edge.
Higher trade frequency (20-100+ trades/day) makes each loss statistically trivial and easier to cut.
Review recordings of your own trades only (not whole sessions); note new bot behaviours you observe.
Simulators often give unrealistic fills (filled at the far side, instant fills); trade small live early.
Fees as % of notional can kill short-term strategies; check fee structure versus holding period before choosing a venue/prop firm.
Counterparty risk: keep only ~5% of funds per exchange and pull funds at the first sign of exchange trouble.
Trading many different order books (thin/fast vs thick) builds transferable execution skill.
notes: Crypto fund manager in South Korea; describes funding-basis trades, cross-exchange arbitrage, the Korean 'kimchi premium' (no shorting/leverage for retail) and correlated-pair stat arb on perps.

style: retail part-time day trader; contest winner (21-day CWT/Trade The Pool contest)
edge_principles: Universe filter: trending mid/large caps that move 10-20% a day and are gapping; avoid penny stocks (commissions/spreads).
Trade the same small weekly watchlist (about four names) all week to learn their behaviour instead of chasing new tickers.
Risk ~1% per trade; trade only the first 10-15 minutes for the 1:1 strategy.
If too happy or too upset after the day (or after 3 trades), skip trading the next day.
When a strategy fails for several days in the current regime (gap-and-go lost ~8k in contest week 1), switch to the playbook setup suited to conditions.
Price action over lagging indicators (moving-average signals gave him many false alarms).
Holding winners to the close (no profit target) produced the contest win, but in normal trading he now takes profits near resistance to avoid giving back 3-4R winners.
notes: Contest winner; two setups: 1-minute opening-range breakout on gappers (1:1) and a resistance short after a big-move day followed by a pause day (3-4R).

style: ex-CBOT/institutional options broker, ex-prop options trader; founder of One Option (OptionStalker); top-down RS day/swing trader
edge_principles: Top-down: the market is ~65% of the decision; get the market right, then pick the stock with relative strength/weakness, then choose the vehicle (stock or option strategy).
Relative strength vs SPY reveals institutional accumulation; RS longs lose little if market timing is early and accelerate when the market turns.

Low-probability day filters (cut size and trade count): choppy low-volume overlapping candles, inside day vs prior day, price inside the first-hour range, day after a monster move, ahead of jobs/FOMC.
Do not buy breakouts at the high of day; wait for an orderly dip (overlapping candles, light volume, gains retained) - stacked red candles on heavy volume mean a reversal, not a dip.
Valuation-based shorting fails in bubbles; use fundamentals for awareness and technical breakdowns (lower highs, heavy-volume breaks) for timing.
Size by conviction in market conditions: add to winners on trend days in a trending market, trim in compression.
Exit signs near highs: bearish engulfing/hammers at new highs, overlapping candles on the rally, market double top before major news.
Breaks of descending trend lines (connecting lower highs) are more reliable than breaks of ascending lines connecting highs.
Seasonality: weak late Aug-Sep; failure to rally into year-end is a warning.
New traders: trade one share until win rate > 75% for 3 months before adding size or options.
notes: Veteran relative-strength trader/educator. Concrete: RS dip-buy alert (RS goes negative then positive again with orderly pullback), wait-for-retrace after big-volume daily breakouts, bull put spreads after volatility spikes.

style: retail full-time discretionary swing trader and scalper (Australian equities, FX, indices); CFTe; mentor
edge_principles: Treat trading as a business: a short written business plan (vision, goals, resources, SWOT, action list) above the trading plan, plus a separate trading-psychology plan for handling emotional triggers.
Act as an 'employee' of the trading business with a job specification (if-then rules), monthly performance reviews and accountability (family/future self).
No P&L targets in the first live year (break-even is success); set P&L goals only after years of stable stats (e.g. 65% win rate, 1.8 payoff, profit factor 2.5), then raise risk gradually.
Go live small to experience emotional triggers; 'if you can't make $50 a week you won't make $5,000'.
Swing-trade only when market filters are favourable; a market filter would have protected him in 2008.
Early easy success in a resource bull market gave false confidence - distinguish regime from skill.
Match timeframe to temperament (fast decision makers scalp; analytical types swing); scalping took him 5-6 years to become consistent vs 1.5-3 typical for swing.
Trade the hours with the best liquidity and stop (he scalps ASX until ~12:30 local).
notes: Business-plan / process episode. Mentions Elliott wave wave-4 pullback swing entries early in career but no concrete current setup.

style: retail full-time multi-timeframe technical trader (Chart Guys); stocks, crypto, cannabis sector
edge_principles: Timeframe pairs as fractals: 5-min with 1-hour for stock day trades, 15-min with 4-hour for 24h markets, daily with weekly for swings; match the pair to the instrument's volatility.
In euphoric blue-sky breakouts lock in profits along the way; past pumps (cannabis, 3D printing, crypto) all gave back 90%+.
Bubble checklist: blue-sky all-time highs + huge gains in a short time + euphoria including non-market friends asking about it.
Scale in and out so no single decision is all-or-nothing; frame partial exits positively.

Correlations (e.g. DXY inverse to BTC) are temporary puzzle pieces; drop them when they stop working. Short-term correlations break when a name hits key support/resistance - a tell for relative strength.
Always ask what the bull and the bear are thinking on each chart to avoid tunnel vision.
Fixed dollar risk per trade (size from stop distance), a daily loss cut-off, and a daily target ('day maker').
In an unfamiliar regime (2022 bear) trade smaller and observe to learn it; in bear markets weak sectors fall first and strong ones roll over later.
New traders: stay off 1-2 minute charts; start with swing timeframes.
notes: Multi-timeframe price-action trader. Concrete ideas: 5-min trend flip marking the hourly higher low, first 5-min oversold dip-buy in breakout markets ('back burner'), relative-strength-at-support entry when the stock stops making new lows while QQQ does.

style: retail part-time trader (ex-boom-bust commodity trader; now SPX credit spreads)
markets: SPX options, formerly commodity futures and stocks
edge_principles: Probability and edge are different: high-probability option selling still loses without loss control.
Hard daily loss limit (~1% of account; aiming for ~0.25-0.33%); close the troubled side at the limit - a single uncontrolled loss destroys consistency.
Shorting parabolic moves early is lethal (parabolas accelerate at the end); a shallow consolidation then breakout signals another leg.
Do not let a macro ideology (deflationist/inflationist) override your trend model; a simple 10-day moving-average bias would have avoided most of his big losses.
Oversized positions turned a $3M account into large monthly losses ($1M in a month); size so normal moves do not breach the loss limit.
A full-time job can make you more reckless with trading capital ('something to go home to').
Avoid 'data mining' or 'people mining' for opinions that support an existing position.
Option-position stops face liquidity gaps; mitigate by converting short spreads into ratio/hedged structures in emergencies.
notes: Long boom-bust story (shorting crude/copper in 2008 turned ~$75k into ~$3.1M then gave much back). Now trades SPX credit spreads with a ~1% daily loss cutoff; ~29% YTD at recording.

style: quant researcher/RIA (Quantifiable Edges); systematic swing, index timing and VIX models
markets: S&P 500 stocks, SPY, VIX futures/ETPs, treasuries
edge_principles: Combine several uncorrelated systems (mean-reversion swing, VWAP-based SPY, trend timing, treasuries rotation, VIX) so the portfolio curve is smooth enough to allow modest leverage.
Avoid curve fitting: do not add rules to remove past bad trades; keep the bad trades to see real downside; prefer parameters that work across a range.
Use research to set a nightly market bias (bullish/bearish/neutral); only take longs in a bullish bias, shorts in bearish, and only high-probability trades when neutral.
Aggregate many small active studies into one expected-return line and compare actual vs expected to judge overbought/oversold relative to the evidence.
Seasonality ensemble: average stats from several seasonal cuts (day of month, week of year) rather than trusting one.
Regime: nearly all S&P gains since 2003 came during quantitative easing; flat-to-negative during QT.
VIX ETPs (e.g. VXX) decay over time, giving a persistent short bias; separate long-vol models can hedge sell-offs; trade VIX term-structure shape, not just direction.
Log the reason for every trade; his 'hunch' trades were the worst performers.
Never override live model signals; check each trigger for corporate events/bad ticks before placing orders.
Retest old studies and models; do not drop a long-proven model after a rough two months.
notes: Quant swing/index researcher. Concrete testable edges: FOMC-day long after weakness (exit before 14:00 announcement), capitulative-selling breadth (CBI/catapult) in S&P 100 uptrend stocks, short-term pullback studies above the 200-day.

guest: Hosts recap (Ian Cox, Tessa Dao) + listener voices
style: host recap / listener compilation
edge_principles: Common traits of featured guests: a personal strategy fitted to their temperament, a strong reason (why), persistence through blowups, hard work, mentorship and accountability.
After big losses, shrink size drastically but stay engaged rather than switching to paper only.
Patience to wait for a well-rehearsed A setup justifies bigger size when it appears; ignore missed moves outside your system.
Keep other income while proving consistency part-time; financial pressure leads to reckless trades.
Implement one or two ideas at a time as small actions rather than accumulating untested knowledge.
notes: Recap episode summarising earlier guests (ep245, 249, 254, 255, 257, 258, 259, 260, 266, 267) and listener reasons for trading. No new setups.

style: retired money manager; systematic all-weather trend following and sector/index timing
markets: sector ETFs, S&P futures, index options, diversified futures, Bitcoin futures
edge_principles: Fill drawdown 'potholes' by adding uncorrelated strategies; aim for pairwise correlations roughly between -0.2 and +0.2.
Size every position continuously so risk and volatility per position stay capped (e.g. ~0.5% risk, ~0.3% equity volatility per futures position); balance strategies by volatility.
Think in terms of the next 1000 trades, not the next one; a couple of big trend trades make the year.
Design the system to fit your own objectives, temperament and account size rather than copying someone else's.
Run regular self-awareness checks to stay emotionally neutral; trading should be boring.
Low reliability (win rate in the 30s) is fine if winners are large.
notes: Mostly daily/weekly systematic portfolio material. Testable: asymmetric channel timing on sector ETFs (21-day entry, 50-day exit). Guest cited ~29% YTD (2023) for the all-weather approach; about half of days up.

style: options trader / YouTuber (YES Invests); ensemble of premium-selling and directional options strategies
markets: US equity and index options (SPX, RUT), stocks
edge_principles: Keep a detailed written trading plan (strategy outlines: setup, scanning, management, tracking) and a trading log; have someone else audit the plan for gaps.
Think through scenarios before they happen so a losing trade does not cause decision paralysis (his 2011 oversized RUT iron condor cost ~34% in a day).
Size small; far-OTM high-probability trades still carry large losses when wrong.
Judge strategies by expected return (win rate x avg win vs loss rate x avg loss), not win rate; high win rates often hide negative expectancy and feed the disposition effect.
Limiting drawdowns beats chasing big years: lower average return with no losing years can compound faster.
If many directional trades get stopped out at once, the market is turning; pause new risk until it settles.
Look for reasons to say no; only trade when the evidence clearly favors it.
Keep offsetting beta-weighted deltas as a hedge against sudden market capitulation.
notes: Mostly options and mindset. Guest cited CAGR ~21.3% 2007-2022 vs S&P ~8.5%. Only setup recorded: selling volatility when implied > realized (variance risk premium); not testable with MCF stock data.

style: global macro CIO (ex head of macro at Greenlight Capital); discretionary rates/FX/vol
markets: US treasuries, rate futures, FX, equity volatility, large-cap stocks
edge_principles: Trade the Fed's reaction function, not the data itself: ask how the Fed will respond to a release.
Weigh data comprehensively; any single series can support any story.
Fade extreme market reactions to data points that historically do not move the Fed; such moves often fully retrace within hours or a day.
Keep trade structures simple; avoid clever structures (e.g. knock-out options) where being very right pays nothing.
For a big theme (AI), prefer quality companies with strong balance sheets that also benefit from the theme over narrative pure plays prone to deep drawdowns.
Stay nimble; change views when facts change.
notes: Mostly macro/political commentary (Fed policy, fixed-rate borrowers insulated from hikes, AI and jobs). One loosely specified tactical idea: fade data-release overreactions. Low MCF relevance.

style: performance/mindset coach (NLP-based 'mental operating system'); not a trader
edge_principles: Write a long inventory of results you want but lack (aim ~100 items) to surface unconscious limiting beliefs.
Ask 'when did I decide this?' rather than 'why' to locate the origin of a habit.
Phrase instructions positively; the unconscious handles negations poorly.
Set up explicit rewards for hitting performance targets so the habit is reinforced.
Cut news and social media consumption; choose deliberately what you focus on.
notes: Episode file title is '275: William Lam' (list key ep274). Pure mindset/NLP content; no trading setups.

style: ex-CME equity risk officer, finance PhD and Carnegie Mellon faculty; quantitative buy-the-dip trader
markets: equity index futures (S&P, Nasdaq), leveraged index ETFs, VIX
edge_principles: Good traders are good risk managers; the best manage the whole book (gamma, theta, vega, event risk), not just direction.
Know your probabilities at every moment of a trade; they change after every tick (poker-odds analogy).
Build the distribution of forward returns after your entry (1-min, 5-min, 1-day...) and use percentiles to decide exits: a favorable move at the ~95th percentile is a good place to take profit.
Simple quant tools: streaks (N moves in a row), price vs mean/median, cycles, distribution of forward returns given conditions.
Define 'the dip' precisely as distance below a long moving average rather than a vague percent off highs.
Contextualize: a gap down on bad earnings means exit for a fundamental trade but add for a mean-reversion trade; be clear which framework you are in.
Start mean-reversion positions small and scale in; prefer futures to leveraged ETFs because of ETF product risk.
Dips have become faster and more frequent in the modern market, which suits dip buying.
notes: Concrete, testable quant dip-buy on intraday bars (distance below a 1000-bar average) with VIX change as second factor; ~3 signals/week on 1-min bars per guest.
